sentences.text: This dinosaur possessed a beak, long forelimbs with strong claws, slender hind feet, and a crest similar to that of cassowaries.
A 2016 study estimated Chirostenotes to be 2.5 meters long and weigh 100 kilograms.
Other measurements placed the animal at approximately 2.85 meters in length, 90 centimeters high at the hip, and an estimated 50 kilograms in weight.
Its most striking feature was a crest similar to that of cassowaries.
Researchers suggested Chirostenotes may have used its unusually straight second claw to impale soft-bodied prey like grubs, unarmored amphibians, reptiles, and mammals.
The first fossils of Chirostenotes were a pair of hands discovered in 1914 by George Fryer Sternberg in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada.
In 1924, Charles Whitney Gilmore formally described and named the type species Chirostenotes pergracilis based on notes left by Lawrence Morris Lambe.
The holotype specimen of Chirostenotes is the pair of hands designated CMN 2367.
Philip J. Currie and Dale Russell linked previously separate hand, foot, and jaw fossils into a single dinosaur in 1988 using a specimen stored since 1923.
Hans-Dieter Sues renamed the species formerly known as Elmisaurus elegans to Chirostenotes elegans in 1997.
Chirostenotes was likely an omnivore or herbivore, inferred from the beaks of related species.
A 2005 study suggested the elongated second finger with its straight claw was an adaptation for probing crevices.
Researchers suggested Chirostenotes could have fed on soft-bodied prey like larvae, amphibians, reptiles, and unarmored mammals by impaling them with its second claw.
A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and others examined stress fractures and tendon avulsions in theropod dinosaurs to understand their behavior.
A study found that only one of the 17 Chirostenotes foot bones examined for stress fractures actually possessed them.
Chirostenotes belongs to the family Caenagnathidae.
Chirostenotes is classified within the suborder Oviraptorosauria.
Macrophalangia canadensis and Caenagnathus sternbergi are listed as synonyms of Chirostenotes.
Chirostenotes is the only valid genus name for this animal, despite earlier names like Macrophalangia and Caenagnathus being applied to its parts.
It is now known that Chirostenotes was a toothless oviraptorosaur, meaning its jaws were originally misidentified and now belong to a different animal, likely a dromaeosaurid.
Since the late 1980s, most researchers have placed Chirostenotes in its own family, Caenagnathidae.
A 2016 analysis by Funston and Currie found that Elmisaurus belongs within the family Caenagnathidae.
Chirostenotes lived in Alberta, Canada, during the late Cretaceous period approximately 76.5 to 75 million years ago.
Chirostenotes lived during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages, approximately 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
Chirostenotes fossils have been found in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada.
Subsequent studies found that Caenagnathus jaws grouped with traditional caenagnathids but not necessarily with Chirostenotes.
New specimens described in 2015 and 2020 indicated that Chirostenotes is a distinct form from Caenagnathus.
A 2007 cladistic study by Philip Senter cast doubt on whether all large fossils from the Dinosaur Park Formation belonged to the same creature.
Later studies found that the jaws of Caenagnathus grouped with other traditional caenagnathids but not necessarily with Chirostenotes.
